subject: Observability handoff: isolated VPC export topology & SIEM buffer sizing

Subject: Observability export topology & SIEM buffer sizing — Aurelia (private deployment)

Markus / team,

Thanks again for the walkthrough yesterday. As we prep the on-prem handoff for our isolated VPC deployment, the security and ops teams asked for a concise topology and a recommended SIEM buffer sizing model before final acceptance. Key asks:

- A network topology diagram showing where the forwarder/buffer lives relative to the Redwood private nodes (eg: forwarder in customer subnet vs. managed forwarder in enclave).
- Expected egress bandwidth and TLS session counts for typical peak workloads (we provided token/sec estimates in the POC).
- Buffer sizing guidance (disk + memory) so our Splunk team can size HEC ingestion and transient storage if network blips occur.
- Any cryptographic transport choices (mutual TLS, client cert rotation cadence) and where we recommend terminating TLS (customer edge vs. Redwood bridge).

Can you attach a short runbook and an annotated topology so we can loop in our Splunk engineer for capacity validation? We aim to complete acceptance tests by 2027-06-11.

Cheers,
Sylvia Chang

From: Markus Klein <markus_klein@redwood.com>
To: Sylvia Chang <sylvia.chang@aurelia-sys.com>
Cc: Kimberly Park <kimberly_park@redwood.com>, Jonas Weber <jonas_weber@redwood.com>

Subject: Re: Observability export topology & SIEM buffer sizing — Aurelia (private deployment)

Sylvia — thanks, this is a good checklist. Attaching an initial topology and a first-pass buffer model. High level notes up front:

- Topology options:
  1) Customer-side forwarder (recommended): deploy a lightweight forwarder inside the customer VPC that streams to the SIEM endpoint; Redwood pushes compressed/structured batches to the forwarder over mTLS. Pros: customer owns egress, simpler compliance. Cons: customer must run/patch the forwarder.
  2) Managed bridge (Redwood-managed forwarder in an enclave): useful when customer cannot run services. Pros: lower operational lift for customer. Cons: needs strong enclave attestations and dedicated network peering; increases trust boundary.

- Buffer sizing (rule of thumb):
  - Peak traffic estimate: 30k tokens/s avg across a 100ms window -> ~30 events/s per active converse (depends on structured logging). For Aurelia's PO workload, estimate ~1200 events/s peak.
  - Transient buffer requirement for 6 hours of offline retention at peak = ~1200 events/s * 3600 * 6 ≈ 25.9M events. With gzipped JSON avg 1.2KB/event => ~31GB disk + ~2GB mem for index/cache.
  - We recommend 50–80GB disk per forwarder for safety (headroom, retries, compressed chunks).

- TLS & auth: mutual TLS with customer-managed PKI is preferred. We support rotating client certs at 30/90-day cadences; recommend 90 days for customer certs with automated rotation hooks. If customer wants HSM/KMS integration, we can attest via a signed CSR exchange.

Attachments: onprem-export-topology_v1.pdf (annotated), siem-buffer-sizing-spreadsheet.xlsx (numbers and sensitivity knobs), runbook-obsv-bridge.md (draft operational steps).

Can Kimberly or Jonas confirm the runbook ops steps and whether our managed bridge requires additional SOC evidence? We'll also include a short acceptance test checklist.

— Markus
Director, On-Prem Integrations
Redwood Inference

[Attachment: onprem-export-topology_v1.pdf (application/pdf)]

From: Kimberly Park <kimberly_park@redwood.com>
To: Sylvia Chang <sylvia.chang@aurelia-sys.com>, Markus Klein <markus_klein@redwood.com>
Cc: Jonas Weber <jonas_weber@redwood.com>
Date: Fri, 4 Jun 2027 15:30:00 -04:00
Subject: Re: Observability export topology & SIEM buffer sizing — Aurelia (private deployment)

Thanks Markus — I reviewed the attachments and did a quick ops validation. A few operational clarifications and acceptance test steps:

- Forwarder sizing: agree with Markus' 50–80GB disk recommendation. For our standard handoff we require: 2 vCPU / 4GB RAM and 80GB ephemeral disk for each forwarder instance in customer subnet. If customer uses a multi-AZ forwarder pair, double disk and RAM.
- HEC ingestion: Splunk teams typically want sustained connection counts under 500 per HEC cluster. If we see >500 concurrent TLS sessions at peak, we recommend session pooling via a connection proxy (we can supply a lightweight Nginx config).
- Backpressure behavior: if SIEM ingestion fails, forwarder will persist gzipped batches and emit a high-water alert to Redwood telemetry. The runbook includes an automated fallback to S3-compatible encrypted staging (customer-managed) if on-disk space crosses 80%.
- Operational runbook highlights (from runbook-obsv-bridge.md):
  • Start/stop commands, log rotation policy (7d), healthcheck endpoints (/healthz), and recommended Prometheus metrics to scrape (forwarder_queue_len, last_successful_push_seconds).
  • Recovery steps: how to replay preserved batches to SIEM, and how to signal completion to Redwood's control plane for acceptance tests.

Acceptance tests we propose for Aurelia:
1) Network: verify egress connectivity to SIEM endpoint over mutual TLS and validate cert chain.
2) Throughput: run a 30-minute soak at 70% of estimated peak and confirm <1% event loss and <5s median push latency.
3) Failure injection: block SIEM endpoint for 10 minutes and confirm forwarder persists batches and recovers without data loss.

I'll attach the runbook excerpt to this thread. Sylvia — when you have a moment, can you share your Splunk eng's availability next week so we can walk through the buffer numbers and test plan?

Kimberly Park
Senior SRE, Private Deployments
Redwood Inference

[Attachment: runbook-obsv-bridge.md (text/markdown)]
